authored.note: Written for learners from the sources named in each block. It is an explanation, not a recording. Facts listed under each block are checked word for word against those sources.

summary.text: An agent can save something it was told into memory so that a later run can use it. This lab asks whether text saved in memory can later give the agent a permission it was never granted. Its one idea: persisted memory is data that survives into a later run. It can influence a request, but it never becomes a grant. The run is a scripted, deterministic sequence, not an AI reasoning on its own.
facts: This lab teaches one idea: persisted memory is data that survives into a later run.
Recalled text may influence a REQUEST. It does not become a GRANT.

glance.label: What the attacker wants
glance.text: The attacker wants text recalled from memory on a later run to be treated as authority to call the lookup_customer_tier tool.
facts: The attacker wants that later-recalled text treated as authority to call lookup_customer_tier.

glance.label: What the attacker controls
glance.text: Only the bytes of one memory entry in the lab's closed fixture. The browser cannot choose the setting, the grants, the memory body or any trust label.
facts: The persisted memory bytes in the closed fixture.
The browser does not choose profile, grants, memory body, or trust labels.

glance.label: Where it gets in
glance.text: Two separate runs. A WRITE run stores the memory entry; a later RECALL run reads it back. Each has its own run id, so one launch in this Academy mints two ids.
facts: WRITE RUN → MEMORY STORE → LATER RECALL RUN → CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 → REQUEST → CTRL-MCP-001 → HANDLER.

glance.label: Where the trust boundary is
glance.text: Between the recalled memory and the tool. Recalled text may lead the agent to form a request, but server-owned authorization decides the grant. Persisting something does not make it trusted.
facts: Memory may influence a REQUEST. Server-owned authorization determines the GRANT.
PERSISTED MEMORY != TRUSTED INSTRUCTION

glance.label: How the controls handle it
glance.text: CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 only classifies the recalled memory as untrusted data (OBSERVE). CTRL-MCP-001 is the control that decides the follow-on tool request.
facts: CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 classifies recalled memory. It does not grant tools.
CTRL-MCP-001 is the tool PDP.

glance.label: Recalled is not obeyed
glance.text: On the vulnerable ATTACK setting the privileged tool ran. In the lab's own words the memory influenced a request and the vulnerable authorization profile granted it; the memory did not grant the tool.
facts: The recalled memory influenced a request. The vulnerable authorization profile granted the request. The memory itself did not grant the tool.

glance.label: What evidence exists
glance.text: Each launch records a write run and a recall run, the memory id and content hash, the recall run's source_run_id, both decisions and the handler count. The handler count is the authoritative record of execution.
facts: Correlation: memory.id + content.hash + source_run_id + destination run.id + agent id + sequence.
Runtime handler count is authoritative for non-execution. Missing indexed execution is corroboration.

path.label: Memory bytes
path.detail: Text placed in the lab's closed memory fixture.
path.fact: The persisted memory bytes in the closed fixture.

path.label: Write run, then later recall run
path.detail: Two runs with different run ids.
path.fact: WRITE RUN → MEMORY STORE → LATER RECALL RUN

path.label: Persistence is not trust
path.detail: Memory may influence a request; it cannot grant.

path.label: Recall classification
path.detail: CTRL-MEMORY-CONTEXT-001 records OBSERVE (memory_context_is_data). It classifies only.

path.label: Follow-on authorization
path.detail: CTRL-MCP-001 decides whether the requested tool is granted.

outcomes.label: DENY (defended retest)
outcomes.detail: tool_not_granted; the handler does not start.

outcomes.label: ALLOW (vulnerable attack setting)
outcomes.detail: A labelled lab-only fail-open mechanism, not a server grant.

path.label: Tool handler
path.detail: lookup_customer_tier with scope customer:read, only if granted.

path.label: Evidence copy
path.detail: A copy of the telemetry goes to Splunk, which only observes.
path.fact: Splunk does not ALLOW or DENY a follow-on tool.

known.text: The store is deterministic in-process memory, not a vector database.
facts: The store is deterministic in-process memory, not a vector database.

known.text: RETEST DENY is not automatically SAFE. One RETEST is not universal memory-poisoning resistance.
facts: RETEST DENY is not automatically SAFE. One RETEST is not universal memory-poisoning resistance.

known.text: HEC HTTP 200 is not searchable evidence. WRITE READY is not EXPERIMENT READY.
facts: HEC HTTP 200 is not searchable evidence. WRITE READY is not EXPERIMENT READY.

known.text: Missing mcp.started is not independent proof of prevention.
facts: Missing mcp.started is not independent proof of prevention.

known.text: CTRL-MCP-001 is a lab allow-list, not production MCP IAM.
facts: CTRL-MCP-001 is a lab allow-list, not production MCP IAM.

terms.text: Storing text does not make it trustworthy. It is still untrusted data when it is read back.
Reading something from memory is not a permission to do what it says.
Two runs with their own run ids, linked by the recall run's source_run_id. One launch here mints both.
terms.fact: Treat write run.id and recall run.id as different identities linked by source_run_id.

terms.text: RAG is information retrieved within one run. Memory is state that survives into a later run.
terms.fact: RAG = retrieved external/contextual information in one run. MEMORY = persisted state surviving into a later run.

terms.text: OBSERVE means the control recorded and classified the memory. It is not a permission.

defender.text: Keep the grant on the server. Memory may influence a request, and server-owned authorization decides the grant. Sanitizing memory, trusting a scanner, asking Splunk or letting a model decide authority are the approaches the lab says not to rely on.
facts: Memory may influence a REQUEST. Server-owned authorization determines the GRANT.
Not: sanitize all memory, block every suspicious string, trust a scanner, ask Splunk, let an LLM decide authority.

lines: Do not label SAFE, TRUSTED, APPROVED, or BENIGN.
No privileged follow-on was observed in this specimen. That is an observation, not proof that the stored content is safe.
The memory itself did not grant the tool.
